origin: Michel Foucault argued that power produces subjects rather than merely forbidding them; that knowledge is bound to the institutions which examine, archive, and train; that the body is an object of discipline and of biopolitics; that discourse governs what may be said; that history has no destination; that the modern West put sex into speech rather than liberating it; and that the self is an exercise.

marks.label: Power produces subjects
marks.line: Power is not only a prohibition. It produces the kinds of people who can be forbidden, examined, and ruled — subjects, not merely the objects of a law.
marks.gloss: He discovered your mother, renamed her a diagram, and billed the seminar. The claim is real enough: a law that only says no cannot explain how anyone becomes the sort of person the law can address. Families, parishes, and regiments already knew that. They called it bringing someone up. If power makes you, so does gravy. One of these still has a claim to be true. The other has a reading list.

marks.label: Discipline makes individuals
marks.line: Discipline does not crush the individual from outside. It manufactures individuals by distributing bodies in space, time, exercise, and rank — in the school, the barracks, the factory, and the prison.
marks.gloss: The school, the barracks, the factory, and the prison share techniques. They also share lunch. He drew that overlap and gasped, as if a timetable were a coup. The claim is that the individual is an output of drill, not a soul the drill then meets. Shared form is not shared guilt. Civilisation drills people because undrilled people cannot read, march, or ship. A child who cannot sit still is not a martyr of micro-physics. He is late for arithmetic.

marks.label: Power at the extremities
marks.line: Do not look for power as a prize stored in the palace. Study it at its extremities: the gesture, the timetable, the file, the little procedures that train a body.
marks.gloss: Study the timetable if you like. The palace still exists. He found power in the file clerk and forgot the Tsar, which is a very indoor theory of politics. The claim is that sovereignty is the least interesting place to look. The trouble is scale. A hall monitor and a secret policeman both use paper; only one of them can ruin a country. A philosophy that cannot tell them apart will sit out an actual tyranny and still feel busy.

marks.label: Resistance is interior
marks.line: Where there is power there is resistance. Resistance is never exterior to power; it is born inside the relations it opposes, and has no pure outside from which to strike.
marks.gloss: Then there is no outside, which is a very convenient inside. The claim is that every no is already a move in the game, so you cannot leave the game, you can only invert a relation. The older hope was a soul that could refuse the world, not a special issue. If resistance is always already power, the seminar is not the underground. The underground had worse coffee and, occasionally, a door.

marks.label: Government of populations
marks.line: Governmentality is the conduct of conduct: the art of acting on other people’s actions. Sovereignty, discipline, and the government of a population are three forms of that art, not a single throne.
marks.gloss: States govern populations. He named the job description and the room went quiet, as if census and grain were a scandal. The claim is that modern rule is less a king’s sword than an art of managing a living mass — births, health, circulation. They are the job. The 1978–79 lectures then wander into German ordoliberals and Chicago, as if markets had been hiding behind a curtain. The left filed that under unfinished. Everyone else filed it under he noticed the century had a cost, and the cost was not a timetable.

marks.label: The medical gaze
marks.line: The clinic’s medical gaze does not simply find a disease waiting in the body. It constitutes the patient as a case — a visible, classifiable object of knowledge.
marks.gloss: He watched a doctor look at a lung and discovered looking. The claim is that the clinic does not uncover a disease so much as make a case: a body that can be seen, named, and filed. Fine as a note on paperwork. Fatal as a theory of medicine. Empiricism with a white coat is why you are not bled for humours. If looking is already domination, closing your eyes is not a method. The tumour, untheorised, remains on the scan.

marks.label: The examination
marks.line: The examination is a ritual that objectifies a person and archives them in the same gesture. It makes a case of you, ranks you, and files the result.
marks.gloss: He sat an exam, then theorised the exam. The claim is that testing is not a measure of what you know so much as a ceremony that turns you into a record. Tests exist because some answers are wrong, and a civilisation that will not say so will still rank people — by charm, cousinage, and volume. He made failing a ceremony of power. The rest of us called it Tuesday. Two plus two is not a vibe, and the archive of who got it right is not a police file. It is a school.

marks.label: The archive of statements
marks.line: The archive is not a warehouse of facts. It is the system of rules that governs which statements may appear, be repeated, or disappear in a given period.
marks.gloss: He sat in the Bibliothèque Nationale and then defined archive so that librarians could not recognise the building. The claim is that what can be said is already policed by a system, not stored as fact waiting on a shelf. If that is all there is, his own sentences are just more police. He wrote as if they weren’t. The stamp on the card still works, and so does the book that answers back.

marks.label: Madness is partitioned
marks.line: Madness is not simply found as a natural kind. It is historically partitioned — confined, medicalised, silenced — by the institutions that claim to know it.
marks.gloss: Some people are ill. He put them on a ship of fools and called it history. The claim is that ‘madness’ is a changing partition, not a thing in nature waiting to be named. Useful against treating the asylum as eternal. Reckless if it forgets the illness. Uppsala’s examiner found brilliant essayism and not empiricist history: the most expensive way to say lovely, but. Fill the ward with metaphors and you still have a ward. The metaphor belongs in the book. The doctor belongs in the room.

marks.label: The episteme
marks.line: An episteme is the historical a priori of an age: the underground grid that decides, before any particular science, what will count as a statement.
marks.gloss: He announced the rules of what can be said, from inside the rules of what can be said, and did not giggle. The claim is that each age has a hidden grammar of knowledge — Renaissance resemblance, classical representation, then the figure of Man — and that sciences do not simply accumulate. A gorgeous three-act. The heckle is that some statements do not wait for the scenery. Two plus two did not wait for an episteme. Neither did the harvest. The harvest has a deadline, which is a kind of truth the seminar never quite scheduled.

marks.label: From scaffold to cell
marks.line: Modern punishment shifts from the spectacle of the scaffold — the body as public example — to the timetable of the cell, where the body is trained rather than displayed.
marks.gloss: He opened with the horses. Undergraduates never recover. Then he asked you to mourn the timetable, as if not drawing and quartering people were a loss of authenticity. The claim is that the cell is not kinder so much as a different technology: it works on the days of a life instead of an afternoon of pain. Preferring the cell to the scaffold is not a conspiracy. It is called progress, and also Tuesday. The horses were not a pedagogy. They were horses.

marks.label: Docile bodies
marks.line: A docile body is one that can be used, transformed, and improved. It is produced by shared techniques of space, time, exercise, and rank.
marks.gloss: Space, time, exercise, rank: he found the school day and gasped. The claim is that a useful body is not born, it is made — by rooms, clocks, drills, and places in a line. The ordinary word is habit. His word is diagram. Habit is how you get a regiment that holds, a factory that ships, a child who can read. A diagram is how you get a citation. One of these gets a bus to arrive. The other gets a waitlist. A child who can read is not a docile body in the interesting sense. He is a child who can read.

marks.label: The panopticon
marks.line: Bentham’s panopticon — a circular prison in which one unseen watcher can see all — is offered as the diagram of a society that trains people by the mere possibility of being seen.
marks.gloss: Bentham’s circular prison was barely built. Foucault built it in every syllabus — the neatest real-estate trick in French letters. The claim is that modern society does not need a whip if it can install the feeling of an eye: you watch yourself because you might be watched. We already knew God and the neighbours were watching. We called it the village, then conscience. He called it a machine and sold the machine to people who had demolished the village and needed a villain with a floor plan.

marks.label: Visibility is a trap
marks.line: Visibility is a trap. Full light captures better than darkness, which once protected; being seen becomes a means of control rather than a guarantee of truth.
marks.gloss: A fortune cookie for anyone with a camera, and a real line. The claim is that Enlightenment light — see everything, hide nothing — is a capture device, not a liberation. Darkness protected the thief as well as the mystic. The leap is the problem: being seen is treated as already guilt, so the only innocent life is an unlit one. He made visibility a trap and then sat for the photograph. The village managed both. You were seen, and you were still allowed a door.

marks.label: Soul as prison of the body
marks.line: The soul, in this account, is not a substance waiting inside the flesh. It is the effect and instrument of a political anatomy: the soul is the prison of the body.
marks.gloss: Christianity said the opposite and built hospitals: the soul as the thing the body is for, not a lock on it. The claim is that ‘soul’ is what discipline invents so that a body can be judged, trained, and held responsible. He inverted a sentence and called it a political anatomy. If the soul is only a prison, the discovery is a typo with tenure. Scare quotes do not set a bone. They make a poor anaesthetic and an excellent seminar title.

marks.label: Biopolitics
marks.line: Biopolitics is power that takes charge of life itself — birth rates, health, populations, species — rather than the old right of the sword to take life or let live.
marks.gloss: Power that keeps you alive is the villain now. He watched a state count births and heard a coup. The claim is that modern rule no longer shows itself mainly as the right to kill; it manages life as a mass — fertility, hygiene, longevity. The older right of the sword at least had the courtesy to be visible. A census is not a massacre. Sanitation is not a sword. A theory that cannot tell them apart will treat the drain as a politics. Try cholera as the footnote. It remains a very persuasive critic, and it does not need a diagram.

marks.label: The author-function
marks.line: The author is a function of discourse: a principle of thrift that limits what a text can mean by attaching it to a name, a legal person, and a corpus.
marks.gloss: Barthes killed him. Foucault made him a function. The claim is that ‘the author’ is not a person with a pen so much as a rule for reading: this name, this oeuvre, these meanings allowed. The function then became the most-cited author of books in the humanities. You cannot liquidate the author and keep the royalties in influence. Someone wrote the book. Credit is a receipt, not a bourgeois plot. He would like you to misplace it.

marks.label: To have no face
marks.line: The writer of an archaeology should have no face, and should not be made to remain the same. The work is a method, not a portrait of a self.
marks.gloss: He asked for no face, meaning: do not pin this method on a biography or demand that the next book match the last. The photograph is in the course packet. Do not ask who I am: then stop answering from the most universal pulpit in France. Anonymity is a luxury of people whose names already travel. The poster travelled further, which is what happens when you refuse a face and keep the chair.

marks.label: Discourse is rarefied
marks.line: Every society selects, organises, and redistributes discourse. Commentary, the author, and the disciplines are among the procedures that rarefy what may be said.
marks.gloss: Every society picks what may be said. He discovered the guest list and called it rarefaction, as if a culture were a crime scene. The claim is that speech is not free flow: it is thinned by commentary, by names, by the disciplines that decide who may talk. The rest of us called it manners, the canon, or blasphemy — the ordinary names for not letting everything in. He delivered the news from the chair he had just won. Either a joke he was in on, or the French for we have a list and a nicer font.

marks.label: A face drawn in sand
marks.line: Man, as both object and subject of the human sciences, is a recent invention — a face drawn in sand at the edge of the sea, liable to be erased.
marks.gloss: France bought the book. The claim is that ‘Man’ is not a given. It is a late figure of knowledge, invented when the human sciences needed a centre, and it can go. Humanists have been standing on the beach with a bucket ever since, waiting for a tide that is a metaphor. The face is still there. It has a name. It has a mother. If man is recent, so is the seminar that announced his funeral. Both can be late. The tide, unhelpfully, is still a tide.

marks.label: Statement, not sentence
marks.line: A statement is not a sentence that simply refers to the world. It is an event in a discourse: something that appears under rules, can be repeated, and has a place.
marks.gloss: He decided a sentence does not point at the world so much as occur inside a discourse. The claim is that meaning is a matter of position and repeatability, not of a word hitting a thing. The world, unconsulted, continued. If reference is naïve, so is the footnote, and so is the butcher’s bill. The enunciative function does not pay either. Take the boring sentence that points. The butcher, inconveniently, exists.

marks.label: Archaeology of knowledge
marks.line: Archaeology describes the rules of what can appear in a given period. It refuses history as a march of influences, intentions, and great minds handing truth down the line.
marks.gloss: A method book nobody loves, written mostly in Sidi Bou Saïd, which is how you know the method is working. The claim is that you should map the rules of what can be said, not tell a story of genius influencing genius. After the rules, you still have to explain why this army moved and that harvest failed. Discursive formation is not a weather report. When the roof leaks, someone is still to blame, and it is not a statement.

marks.label: Genealogy of the present
marks.line: Genealogy, after Nietzsche, is a history of the present. It traces descent and emergence — accidents, captures, reversals — not a destiny that was ripening toward us.
marks.gloss: Nietzsche at least had the good taste to like the strong. Foucault’s genealogy is a solvent: pour it on tradition, nature, the family, and watch them unstick into accidents. The claim is that what looks given — the prison, the self, the norm — has a dirty, contingent past, and that past does not aim at us. Useful against destiny-talk. Useless when you still have to stand somewhere. Someone has to see far enough to plant, and to know whose field it is.

marks.label: Infamous lives
marks.line: Power leaves a record of the obscure. Internment papers, lettres de cachet, and police files catch lives that had no other monument, in the light of the apparatus that seized them.
marks.gloss: Good. Read the files. The claim is that the archive of power is also a portrait of people who would otherwise have left no name — the interned, the denounced, the briefly lit. He found the obscure in the carton and made a priesthood of the finding. The infamous get a theorist, the theorist gets a method, the method gets disciples who have never opened a box. Documents are not improved by being called flashes of power. They are improved by being read first, preferably before the theory arrives.

marks.label: Power as a policeman
marks.line: Power is not only a Western timetable. In a recently independent state it can be a policeman, an arrest, a force that does not need a diagram to be intolerable.
marks.gloss: He was not in the Latin Quarter in May. He was in Tunisia, teaching, writing the Archaeology, and watching a policeman in a recently independent state. The claim, if you take the years seriously, is that some power is still a gun and a cell, not a school timetable. The disciples still talk as if 68 happened to him in Paris. The policeman, unlike the diagram, has a gun. The postcard was never assigned.

marks.label: The university as apparatus
marks.line: After 1968 the university itself is an apparatus that produces authorised intellectuals: a place that makes names, publics, and the right to speak.
marks.gloss: He mapped how institutions make subjects from inside the institution that makes names. The claim is that Vincennes and then the Collège are not a view from nowhere: they are machines for authorised speech. To his friends this is not a contradiction. To everyone else it is the joke: storm the Bastille, be given a flat there, call the flat an apparatus. The vulgar word is a job. The job came with a pulpit, which is an excellent place from which to theorise pulpits.

marks.label: Against the repressive hypothesis
marks.line: The repressive hypothesis is false. We are not silent Victorians who became free by speaking. The modern West multiplied ways of making sex speak, and called that speech liberation.
marks.gloss: Agreed: the West did not shut up about sex. The claim is that the story ‘they silenced us, we spoke, we are free’ is the wrong story — speech itself was the apparatus, not the jailbreak. He discovered the Victorians talking and called it a hypothesis, which is fair as far as it goes. The sequel he did not stay for is a culture that will not shut up about it and calls the noise liberation. Incitement to discourse is now a content vertical with ads. Some things are private because they are serious. A door that closes remains a technology.

marks.label: We Other Victorians
marks.line: The Victorians did not hush sex. They multiplied its languages — medicine, pedagogy, demography, confession — and installed them in clinics, schools, and the state.
marks.gloss: We Other Victorians. The joke is on the people who thought they had escaped. They built podcasts. The claim is that the nineteenth century did not bury sex; it professionalised it, filed it, taught it, and counted it. He found the medical file, the schoolbook, and the confession, and gasped as if speech itself were the plot. A society that talks less about sex and builds more is not a footnote in a history of avowal. It has railways. Railways remain a stronger argument than a confession.

marks.label: Scientia sexualis
marks.line: The West developed a scientia sexualis: a will to knowledge that extracts a truth of sex through avowal. It is offered against an ars erotica, in which pleasure is an art rather than a confession.
marks.gloss: He split the world into people who confess and people who have an art of love, which is a very French map. The claim is that Western sex is a science of truth extracted by talking — priest, doctor, couch — not a craft of pleasure. Wanting a truth about the body is not a Christian plot if the body has one. Confession, clinic, and couch are not the same as a policeman. The memoir as mass edition is a market. Markets are not epistemes. They are what you get when you stop pretending desire is a secret and start selling it by the episode.

marks.label: Ethics of the self
marks.line: Volume I sketched a history of sexuality as a six-book series on children, women, perverts, and population. The late volumes recast the problem as Greco-Roman ethics: sexual conduct as a practice of the self rather than a law of desire.
marks.source: The Use of Pleasure / The Care of the Self, 1984
marks.gloss: He sold a six-book raid on the bourgeoisie and delivered the Greeks. Allowed to change his mind. The claim of the late work is that the interesting question is no longer how power made us confess, but how an ancient free man gave himself rules for pleasure. He discovered antiquity the way a man discovers a second bottle. Confessions of the Flesh waited until 2018. The product, it turned out, was not the children. It was a syllabus, and a much quieter theory than the one he had sold.

marks.label: Political spirituality
marks.line: In the Iranian revolt of 1978 he saw a political spirituality: a people willing a different regime of truth against the modernising state, not only a transfer of palaces.
marks.source: What Are the Iranians Dreaming About?, 1978
marks.gloss: The articles are real. I can already hear the French laughing, but I know that they are wrong. The claim is that the revolt was not only a change of government but a will to another kind of truth — a spirituality against the Shah’s modernisation. He went twice, heard a sermon, and discovered that will. What arrived was a clergy that did not need his permission. When a philosopher of power meets a theocracy and hears music, believe the theocracy. The laugh could tell a sermon from a state.

marks.label: Care of the self
marks.line: Care of the self is Greco-Roman askesis: diet, letters, examination of conscience. It is work on oneself, not a mood and not the discovery of a hidden inner person.
marks.gloss: Disciples heard a glow-up. He meant exercises. The claim is that the self is something you do — a diet, a letter, a nightly look at one’s appetites — not a pearl waiting under a questionnaire. The spa kept the citation. He discovered Lent, vespers, and not being a slave to one’s hungers, then routed them through the Collège so they would count as thought. The ancients had a city attached. Wellness has a subscription. Guess which one buried its dead with a rite.

marks.label: Parrhesia
marks.line: Parrhesia is frank speech that risks the speaker. It is the courage of truth before someone who can punish you, not a brand of authenticity.
marks.gloss: A Greek practice with a price: say the true thing to the person who can hurt you. The claim is that truth-telling is an act with a body on the line, not a style of being genuine. He cited it from a chair that did not wobble, which is almost too neat, so everyone uses it. He discovered losing the dinner, then named it. If your microphone is safe, it is not parrhesia. It is a take. Takes need a follow button. They do not need a Collège de France.

marks.label: Refuse what we are
marks.line: The political target is not to discover what we are — a true self waiting under the files — but to refuse what we are, the identity that power has installed.
marks.gloss: A real line, 1982. The claim is that liberation is not finding the real you under the clinic and the school; it is refusing the you those places produced. He spent twenty years showing how ‘yourself’ gets installed, then said refuse it. The identity industry heard become yourself and hired a photographer. A theory of refusal that cannot say what is worth keeping — the person, the promise, the child — is a solvent with tenure. Tenure, unlike the self, has a committee.

marks.label: The self is worked
marks.line: The self is not found under a questionnaire. It is worked, as the ancients worked it: a form one gives oneself by exercises, not a secret one reports.
marks.gloss: The ancients had exercises. We have profiles. The claim is that you do not uncover a self, you fashion one — subjectivation as practice, not as confession. He discovered working on yourself and called it a long word for an old job. The older word was character. It did not require a neologism, and it could still be ashamed, which is more than a profile can manage. He would have been unbearable on the internet. The internet cannot leave him alone.

marks.label: From confession to askesis
marks.line: The 1970s mapped Christian and clinical confession as a power that produces a subject by making one speak. The 1980s asked how the ancients examined themselves without that police: as an art of living, not an avowal to an authority.
marks.gloss: The 1970s: you become a subject by avowing to a priest, a doctor, a couch. The 1980s: the Greeks had a look at themselves without that police, as an exercise. The claim is a sequel, not a betrayal — from how power makes you talk, to how a free man might train himself. He discovered prayer and routed it through Athens. It is possible to examine your conscience without a theorist in the room. It is also cheaper than a course.

marks.label: The name as apparatus
marks.line: A name in the humanities can become an apparatus of authorised speech: a canon, a method, a way one is required to talk.
marks.gloss: Foucault 2,521; Bourdieu 2,465; Derrida 1,874. Thomson Reuters counted him the most-cited author of books in the humanities. The claim, applied to himself, is that a name can do the work he assigned to the author-function: it licenses speech. He discovered the name, then became the name. Interior to the apparatus is not a refutation. It is a confession to be read aloud, slowly, to the class that assigned him as the way out. The way out had a waiting list.

marks.label: Diagram outruns the building
marks.line: A diagram of visibility travels further than the building it describes. The panopticon as image outruns Bentham’s prison and becomes a general theory of being watched.
marks.gloss: Bentham designed a prison. Foucault designed a diagram. The profession designed an industry of campus papers, architecture midterms, and op-eds about phones. The claim is that a sketch can govern more lives than a building. He found a prison that was barely built and franchised the floor plan. If every camera is Bentham, then nothing is, and a word that used to mean a building now means a feeling. A prison is a prison. Your phone is a nuisance. The citation is the product. The product ships.

marks.label: Power/knowledge
marks.line: Power/knowledge names a compound. There is no knowledge that is not entangled with power, and no power that does not make a knowledge of what it rules.
marks.gloss: The slash is a whole theory: you never just know, you always also rule, and ruling always makes a knowledge. The English book of that title is a 1980 interview collection, not a monograph he named. Undergraduates say the phrase and sit down. The claim dissolves the old courtesy that knowledge might correct power. He discovered that knowing and ruling keep company. The child’s question remains: if your knowledge is only power, why should I believe you? Children are rude that way. Facts are ruder.

marks.label: The subjugated should speak
marks.line: The imprisoned should speak in their own name. The intellectual’s task is to make a space for that speech, not to represent the prisoner as a cause.
marks.gloss: GIP, February 1971, with Domenach and Vidal-Naquet: let prisoners speak, do not speak for them. The claim is that the universal intellectual who represents the wretched is another apparatus; the job is to get out of the way. Eighteen months at the gate, then self-dissolution. The disciples kept the footnote and lost the gates. A philosopher at the gate is still a philosopher. The prisoners went back in. The footnote did not. Footnotes rarely do.

marks.label: The lecture as institution
marks.line: The public lecture is itself an institution. It authorises a body of thought, gathers a public, and makes a name that can be cited.
marks.gloss: From 1970 to 1984 he held the chair Jules Vuillemin steered into existence. Packed rooms. The claim, applied at home, is that the Collège lecture is not a view from nowhere: it is an apparatus that produces authorised thought. He refused the role of universal intellectual and then occupied the most universal pulpit in French letters. He discovered how institutions subjectivate from the nicest institution in the arrondissement. The analysis is not refuted by this. It is illustrated by this. Filed under jobs for the boys. The boys got the jobs.
